entities.summary: John Peckham was a Franciscan friar and Archbishop of Canterbury from 1279 to 1292. He played a crucial role in the Catholic Church during the late 13th century, navigating the complex web of ecclesiastical politics and theological debates. Peckham's tenure as Archbishop saw the rise of the Franciscan Order and the establishment of the University of Oxford, two institutions that would shape the course of Western Christianity. His leadership also witnessed the emergence of the concept of ' Universalism,' which posited that all souls would be saved, regardless of their social status. Peckham's legacy extends beyond his own time, influencing the development of scholasticism and the rise of the Inquisition. Despite his significance, Peckham's life remains shrouded in mystery, with few accounts of his personal life and experiences. Nonetheless, his impact on the Catholic Church and Western civilization is undeniable. The 1292 canonization of John Peckham by the Catholic Church marked a significant turning point in the history of the Franciscan Order, solidifying its place in the pantheon of Christian saints.
